parts.intro: You will hear a woman phoning a water-sports centre to book kayak lessons.

turns.text: Good morning, Larch Bay Paddle Centre, Marcus speaking. How can I help you?
Oh, hello. I'm ringing about kayak lessons. I picked up one of your leaflets at the library, and I'd like to book something for myself, and possibly for my husband as well.
Of course. Have either of you done any kayaking before?
Only once, on holiday, and that was years ago. So I'd say we're really complete beginners.

OK. Well, we run two courses for adults. There's the Intermediate course, but that's for people who can already get back into a boat on their own after a capsize, so I wouldn't recommend that one for you. For complete beginners it's the Starter course. That's four sessions, one a week.
The Starter course sounds right, then. Four weeks is fine for us.
Great. Let me take a few details. Can I have your name, please?
Yes, it's Helen Prothero.
Could you spell the surname for me?
Sure. It's P-R-O-T-H-E-R-O.
Thank you. Now, the next Starter course... we have one beginning on Saturday the 7th of July, but I'm afraid that one's already full. The following one begins a week later, on Saturday the 14th.
The 14th is fine. We're away on the 7th anyway, visiting my sister.
Perfect. The sessions start at a quarter past nine... sorry, no, I'm reading last year's timetable. They've changed it for the summer. They start at 9.30 and finish at around half past eleven.
9.30. That's no problem.

When you arrive, please don't go to the main car park. People often park there and then have to walk all the way round the bay. Come straight to the boathouse, which is the green building next to the café.
The green building next to the café. Got it.

You'll need to bring a change of clothes, because you will get wet, I can promise you that. And bring a towel as well. You don't need to bring a buoyancy aid or a helmet; we provide all the safety equipment.
What about shoes? I don't have anything special.
Old trainers are fine. Just nothing that will come off easily in the water, so no sandals.
And could I ask about costs? The leaflet mentioned some extras.

Yes. The course itself is £96 per person, and that includes the boat and paddle. Then there are a few optional extras. Wetsuit hire used to be £5 a session, but it went up this year, so it's now £6 per session. Most people do hire one, especially early in the season when the water's still cold.
£6 a time. OK, I think we'd want that.

Then there's the photo package. One of our instructors takes pictures from the shore during the last session, and you get those plus a short video of you out on the water. People often buy it as a gift.
That sounds fun. Is there any kind of discount available? My husband asked me to check.
We don't offer group discounts, I'm afraid, not even for families. But there's ten per cent off for students, if you show a valid card on the first day.
Ah, neither of us is a student, unfortunately. And what happens if we need to cancel?

If you cancel 48 hours or more before the first session, you get a full refund. If it's later than that, we can only offer you a place on a later course. I know some centres only ask for 24 hours' notice, but we need two days to offer the place to someone on our waiting list.
That seems fair. And if the weather's bad?
If there's a strong wind warning, we'll text you by seven in the morning and move the session to the following week, so you won't lose anything.
Lovely. I'll talk to my husband tonight and call back to confirm both places.
No problem. I'll hold your place until Friday. Thanks for calling, Helen.

parts.intro: You will hear a volunteer guide giving an introductory talk to visitors at a botanic garden.

turns.text: Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome to Hollins Vale Botanic Garden. My name's Ruth, and I'm one of the volunteer guides here. Before you head off to explore, I'd like to give you a short introduction to the garden and point out a few things you won't want to miss.

First, a little history. Many visitors assume the garden was started by wealthy collectors to show off exotic plants brought back from overseas. That did happen, but only much later. The garden was actually founded in 1824 by a group of local doctors, who needed a reliable supply of medicinal plants for the town hospital. A school for training gardeners was added about fifty years after that, and it still runs today.

Now, what's new this year? You may have read that the café is moving to a bigger building by the lake. That is going to happen, but not until next spring. And some of you may remember that there were plans for a new main entrance on Mill Road; those were turned down by the council, so you'll still come in the way you did today. The big news is that the Palm House, our Victorian glasshouse, reopened in April after three years of repairs, and it's looking wonderful.

A word about how we'd like you to behave in the garden. Unlike a lot of gardens, we actually encourage you to walk on the lawns, so please do enjoy them. Feeding the ducks is fine too, as long as you use the seed sold at the kiosk rather than bread. But please don't touch anything in the medicinal beds near the entrance. Some of those plants can irritate the skin quite badly, and we've had a few unhappy visitors.

If you'd like to learn more, we used to run guided walks only at weekends, but now our volunteers lead a free walk around the whole garden every morning at eleven, starting from the sundial. There's also a bird-watching walk on the first Sunday of each month, but that one is run by a separate society and there's a small charge of three pounds.

And finally in this section, the Rock Garden. Most people will tell you that late spring is the best time to see it, when the alpine flowers are out, and it is lovely then. But my own advice is to go straight after rain. The wet stones change colour completely, and the whole place seems to glow. Early morning is pleasant too, but it's often closed for watering until ten.
Right, if you look at the plan of the garden in your leaflet, I'll tell you what you can find in each of the main areas.

Let's start with the Palm House, which I mentioned earlier. As well as the palms, of course, there's a humid corner at the far end with a collection of plants that trap and digest insects. Children love them. The cacti used to be in there too, but they didn't do well in the damp air, so they've been moved.

Next to it is the Walled Garden. It's sheltered and quiet, and we've put benches under the fruit trees with a box of books that anyone can borrow, so it's become a sort of outdoor reading area. Do take a book back to the bench when you've finished.

Down by the water there's the Lake Meadow. Some of you will be sad to hear that the garden's oldest tree, a huge oak that stood by the lake, came down in a storm last winter. But there's something new to see there: a beehive with a glass wall, so you can watch the bees working without any risk of being stung.

Then there's the Woodland Walk, which is the best place to take younger visitors. We've set up a trail with puzzles at ten points along the path, and if they solve them all, they can collect a small badge from the kiosk.

And lastly, the Old Nursery, where young plants used to be grown. That's where the cacti went, and they're much happier there in the dry, sunny glasshouse. There was also a little shop selling wildflower seeds in the nursery, but it closed last year; the seeds are now only sold online.
OK, that's all from me. Enjoy your afternoon, and do come and find me at the sundial if you have any questions.

parts.intro: You will hear two students, Chloe and Ryan, talking to their tutor about a survey project on student travel.

turns.text: Come in, both of you. So, you wanted to talk about your survey project for the research methods module?
Yes. We've decided to look at how students travel to campus, and how long their journeys take.
Commuting. OK. What made you choose that? Was it because the university's been asking for travel data?
People keep saying that, but actually nobody asked us. It's really that we both spend over an hour on the bus every morning, and we wanted to know if that's normal or if we're just unlucky.
Well, a personal interest is a good starting point. And you'll certainly have plenty of people to ask.
That's true, though honestly that wasn't the reason. Anyway, we've brought our first draft of the questionnaire.

Let me have a look. Mm. The questions themselves are clear, and I don't think anything here is too personal; you're not asking for home addresses, which is good. My real concern is the length. You've got twenty-eight questions. People filling this in at eight in the morning will give up halfway through.
We did wonder about that. We could cut the questions about cost, maybe.
I'd aim for about twelve. Think about what you actually need to answer your research question, and cut everything else. If a question is only there because it might be interesting, it should go.
So the questions about which music people listen to on the bus would have to go, I suppose.
I'm afraid so, fun as they are. Now, how are you planning to collect responses?
I suggested putting it online, through the course pages, because it's quick.
It's quick, but response rates for online surveys here are very low, often under five per cent. You'd also only reach students who check their course pages, which isn't everyone.
My idea was to sit in the library with a laptop, but then we'd mainly get people who stay on campus all day.
So in the end we agreed to stand at the three bus stops nearest the campus in the morning, with paper forms. That way we catch people actually arriving.
That makes sense, as long as you keep it short. Did you run a pilot?

Yes, with ten people from our seminar group. The main problem was that several of them read 'journey time' as door to door, including the walk to the stop, while others counted just the time on the bus. So the answers weren't comparable.
Then you'll need to define it on the form. Say clearly 'from leaving home to arriving at the campus gate'.
We were also thinking of comparing our results with something bigger, like the national travel figures.

The national statistics are about people travelling to work, not students, so they're not really comparable. And the bus company won't share its passenger data; others have tried. But last year's group did a smaller study on cycling to campus, and their raw data is in the department archive. You could compare your findings with theirs.
That's a great idea. I didn't know we could use previous projects.
You can, as long as you acknowledge them properly in your report. Their sample was quite small, so be careful about drawing strong conclusions from any differences you find.
Have you got any early results yet, from the pilot?
A few. What surprised us was that price didn't come top. We expected everyone to complain about the cost of bus passes, but only two people mentioned it.

The two things people mentioned most were later buses in the evening, because the last bus leaves at half past eight, and secure places to leave bikes. Apparently bikes keep getting stolen from the racks behind the library.
A couple of people liked the idea of a car-sharing app, and one person wanted more parking, but that was a member of staff, so we'll have to leave that out.
Interesting. Right, so who's going to do what for the final report?
I'm better with spreadsheets, so I'll design the charts.
And I'll write the introduction, because I've already read most of the background literature.

Good. One more thing. You'll need permission before standing at the bus stops with forms, because two of them are on university land. Leave that to me; I'll contact the transport office myself this week, as they tend to reply faster to staff.
Thank you, that's really helpful.
Not at all. Send me the shorter version of the questionnaire by Friday, and we'll meet again next week.

parts.intro: You will hear a lecture on the history of the magnetic compass.

turns.text: Good morning. Today I want to look at an instrument so ordinary that we hardly think about it: the magnetic compass. It's easy to assume that it was invented by sailors, for sailors, but its history is rather more surprising than that.

The story begins with lodestone, a type of rock that is naturally magnetic. Writers in China described its power to attract iron more than two thousand years ago. But the earliest compass-like devices were not used to find the way at all. They were used for fortune-telling, or what historians call divination, and for deciding how buildings and tombs should be positioned. One early design was a spoon carved from lodestone. It was placed on a polished bronze plate, and when it stopped turning, its handle pointed south. It's worth noticing that south, not north, was the direction that mattered in this tradition, which is a useful reminder that the way we think about direction is partly a matter of culture.

So when did the compass go to sea? The key change was the discovery that an ordinary iron needle could be magnetised by rubbing it against lodestone. A magnetised needle was much lighter than a spoon, and it could be floated on a small piece of wood or straw in a bowl of water, where it would turn freely. The first clear written descriptions of compasses being used at sea date from around the eleventh century. They make it plain that the compass was not the sailors' main tool. Navigators relied on the sun and stars, and used the needle only when the sky was hidden by cloud.

In Europe, the compass appears in writing about a century later, and here an important improvement was made: the so-called dry compass. Instead of floating in water, which splashed about on a moving ship, the needle was balanced on a pin, so that it could swing without any liquid at all. Before long, the needle was attached to a card marked with the directions. Interestingly, the earliest of these cards did not show north, south, east and west as we know them. They showed the names of the winds, because sailors in the Mediterranean thought of direction in terms of the winds that blew from each quarter. The decorated star pattern we call the compass rose comes from those cards.

However, the compass was never perfectly reliable, and two problems in particular troubled navigators for centuries. The first was that the iron on board the ship itself, in nails, cannons and later in the hull, pulled the needle away from magnetic north. This effect is known as deviation, and it became much more serious when ships began to be built entirely of iron in the nineteenth century. Engineers eventually corrected it by placing iron balls and small magnets around the compass. You can still see these iron balls, painted red and green, on either side of the compass on many older ships, and visitors often mistake them for decoration.

The second problem is called variation. Magnetic north is not in the same place as true north, the geographic pole, and the difference changes from one part of the world to another, and even from year to year. Navigators learned to measure variation and to record it on charts, so that later ships could adjust their readings. In fact, these records of variation are now valuable to scientists studying how the Earth's magnetic field has changed over time.

Later developments focused on making the compass easier to read in rough conditions. In the nineteenth century, makers began to fill the compass bowl with a mixture of water and alcohol, which does not freeze easily. The liquid slowed down the movement of the card when waves threw the ship around, so the helmsman could actually read it. At around the same time, compass makers began to produce smaller, cheaper models for use on land, by surveyors, soldiers and, eventually, ordinary travellers.

Today, of course, most ships and aircraft navigate using satellite systems. You might expect the magnetic compass to have disappeared, but it hasn't. International rules still require ships to carry one, because it needs no electricity and cannot be switched off by a technical fault. In other words, it survives as a backup for the moment when electronic systems fail. And many of the hill walkers who rely on their phones every weekend would do well to carry one too. Next week, we'll look at the history of measuring longitude.

texts.title: Weekend courses at Riverside Adult Learning Centre

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Bread Baking for Beginners. Spend a Saturday learning to make three kinds of loaf, from a simple white tin loaf to a rye sourdough. Your tutor, Dana Whitlow, runs a small bakery in the old market hall and has been teaching for over ten years. All ingredients and aprons are provided, and you will take home everything you bake. Saturday 10 am to 4 pm. £55.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Furniture Restoration. Learn how to repair loose joints, strip old paint and bring a tired wooden surface back to life. We supply a selection of old chairs and drawers for you to practise on, so please do not bring your own pieces to the first session. Two Sundays, 10 am to 3 pm. £120, or £100 if you book before the end of this month.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Introduction to Digital Photography. Find out what all those buttons on your camera actually do. The morning is spent in the classroom, and after lunch the group goes out along the river path to practise. Please bring your own camera (any type, including a phone with a good camera) and its charger. Saturday 9.30 am to 4.30 pm. £60.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Conversational Spanish. A relaxed course for people who know a little Spanish and want to speak with more confidence before a holiday. Classes are run entirely in Spanish by a native speaker. Runs over two consecutive weekends, Saturday and Sunday mornings. Everyone who attends all four mornings receives a certificate of attendance. £85.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Bicycle Maintenance. Fixing a puncture, adjusting brakes and gears, and keeping your chain in good condition. All tools are provided, though you are welcome to bring your own bike if you would like to work on it. Young people aged 12 to 15 may attend if accompanied by a paying adult. Sunday 10 am to 2 pm. £40.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Garden Design. Whether you have a balcony or a large back garden, this course will help you plan a space that looks good all year. Our designer will look at photos of your garden and suggest planting ideas. The price includes a two-course lunch in the centre's café. Saturday 10 am to 3.30 pm. £75.

Places on all weekend courses can be booked online, by phone or in person at the centre's reception, which is open from 9 am to 7 pm on weekdays. Payment must be made in full at the time of booking. Courses run with a minimum of six participants. If a course does not reach this number a week before it is due to start, it will be cancelled and you will be offered either a full refund or a place on another course.

If you need to cancel your place, please let us know at least ten days before the course begins and we will return your fee, minus a £10 administration charge. We are unable to give refunds for later cancellations, but you may send a friend or relative in your place at no extra cost, provided you tell reception their name in advance.

The centre has a small car park, but spaces cannot be reserved and it is often full on Saturdays because of the market. We recommend using the bus, as the number 14 stops directly outside. Tea and coffee are available free of charge throughout the day on all courses. Participants with particular access needs are asked to contact reception before the course, so that suitable arrangements can be made.

texts.title: Your first week at Hartwell Distribution

paragraphs.text: Welcome to Hartwell Distribution. Your first week is designed to help you settle in safely and get to know the people you will work with. Please read this guide before your first day, and keep it somewhere safe, as you may want to refer to it again during your first few months with us.

On Monday, report to the main reception at 8.15 am, not to the warehouse entrance, even if your normal shifts will start there. You will be met by your induction leader, who will collect your photo pass from security and give you a short tour of the site. Please bring your bank details and proof of your right to work in the country, as the payroll team will need copies before you can be paid.

Most of Monday is taken up with health and safety training. This is compulsory for every new member of staff, including those who will work in the offices. You will learn about fire procedures, safe lifting and the rules for walking through areas where forklift trucks operate. At the end of the session there is a short written test. Anyone who does not pass will repeat the training on Tuesday morning before starting work.

From Tuesday to Thursday you will work alongside an experienced colleague, known as your buddy, who will show you the systems used in your department. Your buddy is not your manager, but they are the best person to ask about day-to-day questions, such as where to find equipment or how to book holidays. Most buddies have been with the company for at least two years and have volunteered for the role, so do not worry about taking up their time.

On Friday afternoon you will have a meeting with your line manager to review the week. This is a good opportunity to raise any concerns and to agree targets for your first three months, which is the length of the probation period for all new staff. At the end of this period your manager will confirm your position in writing, or, in a small number of cases, extend the probation period if more support is needed.

Hartwell Distribution does not have a uniform for office staff, but we expect everyone to dress in a way that is clean, tidy and appropriate for a business setting. Jeans are acceptable on Fridays only. If you meet customers or visitors from outside the company, smart clothing should be worn on those days, whatever day of the week it is.

Warehouse staff are provided with two company polo shirts and a fleece jacket, which must be worn at all times on the warehouse floor. Replacements are free if items become damaged at work; lost items, however, are replaced at the employee's cost. High-visibility vests are kept at the warehouse entrance and must be put on before you go past the yellow line.

Safety boots with protective toe caps are required for everyone who works in or regularly visits the warehouse. The company will pay for one pair a year, up to a value of £60, from our approved supplier. You may choose a more expensive pair if you wish, but you will need to pay the difference yourself.

For safety reasons, jewellery should be kept to a minimum in the warehouse. Rings without stones and small earrings are acceptable, but long necklaces and bracelets must be removed, as they can become caught in machinery. Long hair must be tied back. Staff who wear head coverings for religious reasons should speak to their manager, who will arrange a version that meets safety standards.

If you are unsure whether something is suitable, please ask your line manager or the human resources team before your first shift. Staff who repeatedly ignore the dress code may be sent home to change, and the time taken will not be paid.

texts.title: The story of the travelling library van

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the early years of the twentieth century, a reader who lived in a remote village had very few ways of getting hold of a book. Town libraries existed, but they might be a day's journey away, and most families could not afford to buy books of their own. The solution, which appeared in several countries at roughly the same time, was surprisingly simple: if people could not travel to the library, the library would travel to them. Over the following decades, the idea grew from a handful of experiments into a service that, at its peak, reached millions of readers who would otherwise have had almost no access to books.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The earliest travelling libraries were not vans at all. In some districts, boxes of around fifty books were sent out by rail or by horse and cart to village schools, churches or shops, where a volunteer looked after them for a few months before they were collected and replaced with a fresh selection. Other schemes used horse-drawn wagons fitted with shelves, which visited farms on a regular route. These early services were often run by charities or by individual enthusiasts, rather than by local governments. The choice of books was usually made by a librarian in the nearest town, who had to guess what readers in a distant village might enjoy, and the results were not always popular. A box full of serious history might sit unopened for months, while a single popular novel was passed from house to house until it fell apart.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The arrival of the motor vehicle changed everything. By the 1920s and 1930s, purpose-built library vans with shelves along both sides and a small desk at the back had begun to appear. They could carry far more books than a wagon and cover much greater distances in a day. Crucially, readers could now climb inside and choose for themselves, instead of accepting whatever titles a librarian had packed into a box. For many people, this freedom of choice was what made the service feel like a real library. Some vans also carried newspapers, maps and practical guides on farming and household management, and a few even had a small section of books in the languages spoken by recent immigrants to the area.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Running a van was never an easy job. The librarian was often also the driver, and had to deal with narrow lanes, flooded roads and engines that refused to start on cold mornings. Timetables had to be planned so that the van arrived at each stop at the same time on the same day every two or three weeks, because readers organised their lives around its visits. Librarians who worked on the vans for many years have described how they came to know not just the reading tastes of their borrowers, but their family news, their health problems and even the names of their dogs. Children, in particular, often remembered the van's visits for the rest of their lives, and several well-known writers have said that their love of reading began on its narrow steps.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: This personal relationship turned out to be one of the service's greatest strengths. For elderly or isolated people, the van's visit was sometimes the only conversation they had all week. Librarians would recommend books, pass on messages and occasionally notice when something was wrong, such as a regular borrower who failed to appear at the stop. In this way, the travelling library performed a social function that was rarely written into anyone's job description, and which was difficult to measure in official reports.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: From the 1980s onwards, however, the number of mobile libraries in many countries began to fall. The vans were expensive to buy and maintain, and when local budgets were reduced, they were among the first services to be cut. Supporters argued that the savings were small compared with the value to rural communities, but the number of loans recorded by the vans was often lower than in town branches, and these figures were difficult to argue against. In some regions, the vans were replaced with a postal service, in which borrowers ordered books from a list and received them by mail. This was cheaper to run, but it removed both the pleasure of browsing and the personal contact that many borrowers had valued most.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Yet the travelling library has not disappeared. In recent years, a number of new services have been launched, and many of them look rather different from the vans of the past. Some carry laptops and offer free internet access for people who need to complete official forms online. Others visit schools, care homes and new housing estates rather than villages. In a few countries, libraries have been set up on boats, on bicycles and even on the backs of donkeys, in order to reach communities that no road vehicle can easily get to. Several are now run by volunteers or community groups, much as the earliest schemes were. Whatever form it takes, the idea behind the service remains the same as it was a century ago: that access to books and information should not depend on where a person happens to live.

tasks.prompt: A friend let you stay in their flat while they were away on holiday. Write a letter to your friend. In your letter, thank your friend for letting you stay, describe something you enjoyed doing during your stay, and explain a problem that happened in the flat and what you did about it. Write at least 150 words. You do NOT need to write any addresses. Begin your letter as follows: Dear ......,

bullets: thank your friend for letting you stay
describe something you enjoyed doing during your stay
explain a problem that happened in the flat and what you did about it

key_features: Warm, informal tone throughout (contractions, friendly opening and closing such as 'Best wishes')
Clear thanks for the stay in the opening paragraph
A specific enjoyable activity described with some detail
A problem in the flat explained, plus what the writer did to solve it
One paragraph per bullet point, with a friendly closing line

model_answer.text:
Dear Sam,

I'm writing to say a huge thank you for letting me stay in your flat while you were away. It made my week in the city so much easier, and it was lovely to wake up to that view of the harbour every morning.

The highlight of my stay was the street market you told me about. I went on Saturday morning and ended up spending hours there, tasting food from about six different stalls. I even bought a small painting of the old lighthouse, which is now on my wall at home.

I'm afraid I also need to tell you about a small problem. On my third evening the kitchen tap started leaking quite badly. I turned off the water under the sink and called the plumber whose number was on your fridge. He came the next morning and replaced a worn washer, and I've paid the bill, so please don't worry about it.

Thanks again for being so generous. Next time you visit my town, you must stay with me.

Best wishes,
Maya

tasks.prompt: In many towns and cities today, people do not know the neighbours who live around them. Why is this the case? Is this a positive or negative development? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words.
key_features: Both questions answered: the causes AND a clear positive/negative judgement
At least two developed causes (for example work patterns, frequent moves, technology)
Position stated in the introduction and repeated in the conclusion
Some recognition of the other side (privacy) before the writer's own view
Clear paragraphing with linking words and specific examples

model_answer.text:
In many towns and cities, it is now common for people to live next door to someone for years without ever learning their name. In my view, this situation has several clear causes, and although it brings a degree of privacy, it is on balance a negative development.

The main reason is the way modern people live and work. Many adults commute long distances and work long hours, so they leave home early and return late, with little time to stop and talk in the street. In addition, people move house far more often than previous generations did, especially in cities where most residents rent. When neighbours change every year or two, there is little reason to invest in getting to know them. Technology also plays a part: people now keep in touch with friends and family online, so the street or apartment block is no longer the centre of their social life.

Some would argue that this is not a problem. Living anonymously can mean more privacy and less pressure to take part in local gossip or obligations. For busy professionals, a polite nod in the corridor may be all they want.

However, I believe the disadvantages are more serious. Neighbours who know each other can help in emergencies, for example by checking on an elderly resident during a heatwave or keeping an eye on a house when the owners are away. Communities where people are connected also tend to have lower crime rates, because residents notice and report unusual activity. Finally, loneliness is a growing health issue, and a friendly relationship with the people next door is one of the simplest ways to reduce it.

In conclusion, busy working lives, frequent moves and online social networks explain why many people do not know their neighbours. While this offers some privacy, I believe it weakens the support and safety that strong local communities provide, so it should be seen as a negative trend.
